accuracy.evidence: Checked against NGSS 1-PS4-4 and its clarification (string telephones, flashlight signals and drums as example devices) and the K-2-ETS1-1/3 design-and-test practices; the physics of the cup-and-string telephone (taut string carries the vibration, slack, pinching or contact with an object damps it) against the Science Buddies and IOP string-telephone notes; light travelling in straight lines and being blocked by opaque objects against the Year 3 light guidance; sound spreading round corners and through doors but fading with distance and being masked by noise against the BBC Bitesize KS2 sound pages. The National Curriculum link was corrected to Year 3 light and Year 4 sound after a first draft said Years 1 to 3.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets ideas reported for young children in the Nuffield Primary SPACE research on sound and light: sound stops at a fixed point rather than fading (prediction 1 'just the same', challenge 'stop'), any string works whether loose or not (prediction 2 'a floppy string', 'slack'), touching the string makes no difference ('touch', m2), signals carry meaning without an agreed code (prediction 4 'come here', 'code', m3), light bends round corners like sound (prediction 5 'the torch light', 'straight', p5, m7), and a failed test means the design is hopeless ('quit', m5).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagsignal is about solving a communication problem over distance: a draggable friend on a 1-10 step line hears a green, amber or red voice wave; a string telephone whose sag follows a drag only delivers its travelling shake dot when tight; a three-fault phone (sag, fence post, pinching hand) stops the shake at the first fault on each test so the learner fixes faults in the order the tests reveal them; a night torch scene counts flashes against a code card that Ben lacks until it is shared; and six place cards are sorted into Light or Sound with a reason. flagmedium times sound through materials and flagvib finds what vibrates. lab_distinct passes under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner meets each idea by doing it: saying hello at 2, 4 and 8 steps shows the voice fading to nothing; talking with a floppy string fails and the tight string succeeds; each failed test shows exactly where the shake stopped, so testing becomes the way to improve; flashing 3 times before the code is shared gets 'What does that mean?'; a wrong place choice gives the straight-line or noise reason before the learner tries again.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'just the same' or 'louder' for a far-off voice (the wave turns red and Ben hears nothing), 'both the same' for floppy and tight string (the floppy test fails), 'come here' for 3 flashes without a code (Ben shrugs), and 'the torch light' for a friend round a corner (the card says light is blocked and sound spreads round).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions and eight distinct feedback messages naming the slip: sound fades rather than stopping at a fixed number of steps, a floppy string does not pass the shake, touching stops the shake, builders test and fix rather than give up, a brighter torch still needs a code, flashes mean nothing without a shared code, light goes in straight lines, and noise covers quiet sounds. Answer order rotates.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation reads at FK grade 0.4 in short sentences with words such as shake, string, cup, torch, flash and code; adult text averages 6.4 with the NGSS code named. Lab steps are one or two sentences, each scene has a big status chip (Ben is 8 big steps away, The string is tight, Faults fixed: 2 of 3), and young-class buttons are large.

no_filler.evidence: Gate finds no filler. Each kid paragraph carries one idea (voice fades, the string phone and why it must be tight, a torch code must be shared, light versus sound and testing). Items vary: counting steps away and back, totalling flashes in twos and threes, fixing a floppy string, a squeezed string, a noisy room and a sleeping friend.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots of every step: light theme at the start and after Show me finished, dark theme mid-way through Show me: friends, cups, string, fence post and torch beam fit the 390 px canvas; the step-dot row sits below the friends; the night torch scene keeps white chips readable on the dark sky; place cards shrink their font to fit; controls wrap to two rows and stay reachable.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button: Ben steps back, Ben comes closer, Say hello; Pull tight, Let it go floppy, Talk into the cup; Test the phone and a Fix button for each fault a test reveals; Share the code, Flash the torch, Send; Light and Sound. The canvas aria-label is rewritten with each result (how far Ben is and whether he heard, where the shake stopped, what Ben read). walk.cjs axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
